title: Cupped hands
hook: servers walk the rows and people receive with open, cupped hands

segments.voice: Yesterday, dal: langar kept simple and vegetarian, so no guest has to ask. Your line was everyone can eat this.

Someone offers to pay for your coffee, and what do you say? No, no, I've got it. A friend offers to help you move: oh, don't worry about it. Someone gives you a compliment, and you wave it away before it lands. Giving can be easy while receiving feels awkward. Now sit down in the pangat. A volunteer comes down the row with a basket of warm rotis. When they reach you, you don't grab, and you don't wave them off. You lift both hands together, palms up, cupped like a bowl. And they place the bread right into them.
screen: `NO, NO, I'VE GOT IT.` → `GIVING IS EASY.` → `BOTH HANDS, PALMS UP.`

segments.voice: In langar, the servers walk the rows: one with a bucket of dal, one with a basket of rotis, one with a jug of water. You stay seated. They come to you. And in many gurdwaras you receive the roti the way you receive karah prashad, the sweet offering given at the end of worship: with both hands cupped together. The gesture says a lot without a word. It's open: nothing hidden, nothing held back. It's humble: you're below the giver's hands, waiting. And it's whole: you're not taking with one hand while the other holds your phone. There's a quiet lesson here for anyone who finds receiving hard. Seva teaches you to give without wanting thanks. Cupped hands teach you to receive without embarrassment. Both thin the ego. The one who can only give, and never receive, still keeps a little pride. The Japji has a bigger version. There Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that our actions bring us this body, but the door of liberation opens by God's grace, the nadar, the gracious glance. In that line, the greatest thing is received, not earned. So the cupped hands in the row are practice for something bigger. One more small courtesy. If you don't want more, you don't push the server away; you cover your plate with your hand, or lift a palm. If you do want more, you just hold your hands out again. Nobody keeps count.
screen: `THE SERVERS COME TO YOU.` · `OPEN, HUMBLE, WHOLE.` · `RECEIVE WITHOUT EMBARRASSMENT.` · `GRACE IS RECEIVED, NOT EARNED.` · then, large: `RECEIVE FULLY.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, cupped together like a bowl, and notice how it feels to sit this way, open and empty; some find it peaceful, some strangely hard. Then think of something you were given recently and didn't quite receive, a kindness, a compliment, help you brushed off. Imagine it placed into your hands again, and this time, let it land.
Cupped hands. The way many receive roti and karah prashad in the gurdwara: both hands, open and together, fully there to receive.
Your line: receive fully. Open, humble, and whole, like a bowl. Day one hundred eighteen, done.

screen: `DAY 118 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A SMALL LANGAR AT HOME.`
